The most recent work in this area is the one by Sun et al. [29] presenting RankEF, a T5 model trained to rank code solutions using both execution-based and non-execution-based information. However, Sun et al. do not assess the T5 ranker's classification accuracy, that is, how often it misjudges correct implementations as incorrect or vice versa, leaving open questions about the reliability of LMs as code correctness judges for other tasks (e.g., automated code review). Moreover, their experiments involve relatively old models, making it unclear the extent to which such a methodology would still help companies in cheaply training their own code generators with performance comparable to those of massive LLMs. We present a study addressing these limitations. We train several state-of-the-art SLMs as code correctness judges and assess their ability to discriminate between correct and wrong implementations. We show that modern SLMs outperform RankEF, even without exploiting execution-based information. When used as code rankers, they achieve higher performance gains than RankEF and perform competitively with LLMs 5-25x larger, at a fraction of the cost.

AI.tldr: Modern small language models (SLMs) can effectively judge code correctness and rank code solutions, outperforming prior methods like RankEF without execution feedback and matching performance of much larger LLMs at lower cost.
AI.motivation: While large language models excel at code generation, they are costly to train and deploy; smaller models offer a cheaper alternative but require validation of their reliability in judging code correctness, especially for domain-specific or less common languages.
AI.method: The authors train and evaluate state-of-the-art small language models (SLMs) as code correctness judges, assessing their classification accuracy in distinguishing correct from incorrect code implementations and comparing their performance to RankEF and larger LLMs, without using execution-based information.
AI.result: Modern SLMs surpass RankEF in code correctness classification and ranking effectiveness, achieve higher performance gains when used as rankers, and match the performance of LLMs 5–25x larger despite significantly lower computational costs.
AI.conclusion: State-of-the-art SLMs are reliable and cost-effective alternatives for code ranking and correctness judgment, enabling companies to build efficient in-house code generation systems without relying on expensive large models.

title: Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace: Understanding and Detecting Jailbreak Attacks from Internal Representations of Large Language Models
summary: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a critical security challenge with the widespread deployment of conversational AI systems. Adversarial users exploit these models through carefully crafted prompts to elicit restricted or unsafe outputs, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Jailbreaking. Despite numerous proposed defense mechanisms, attackers continue to develop adaptive prompting strategies, and existing models remain vulnerable. This motivates approaches that examine the internal behavior of LLMs rather than relying solely on prompt-level defenses. In this work, we study jailbreaking from both security and interpretability perspectives by analyzing how internal representations differ between jailbreak and benign prompts. We conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis across multiple open-source models, including GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, and the state-space model Mamba, and identify consistent latent-space patterns associated with harmful inputs. We then propose a tensor-based latent representation framework that captures structure in hidden activations and enables lightweight jailbreak detection without model fine-tuning or auxiliary LLM-based detectors. We further demonstrate that the latent signals can be used to actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time. On an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B model, selectively bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving benign behavior on 94% of benign prompts. This intervention operates entirely at inference time and introduces minimal overhead, providing a scalable foundation for achieving stronger coverage by incorporating additional attack distributions or more refined susceptibility thresholds. Our results provide evidence that jailbreak behavior is rooted in identifiable internal structures and suggest a complementary, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a tensor-based latent representation approach to detect and disrupt LLM jailbreaks by analyzing internal activation patterns, enabling lightweight, fine-tuning-free, and scalable inference-time defense across diverse architectures.
AI.motivation: Despite existing defense mechanisms, LLMs remain vulnerable to adaptive jailbreak attacks through malicious prompts. This work is motivated by the need for more robust, internal model introspection methods that go beyond prompt-level defenses to detect and prevent jailbreaking based on intrinsic model behavior.
AI.method: The authors perform a systematic layer-wise analysis of internal representations in multiple open-source LLMs (GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, Mamba) to identify latent-space patterns associated with jailbreak prompts. They propose a tensor-based framework to capture structural information in hidden activations for lightweight detection and introduce an inference-time intervention that selectively bypasses high-susceptibility layers to disrupt jailbreak attempts.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves 78% block rate on jailbreak attempts and preserves 94% of benign behavior on a weakened LLaMA-3.1-8B model. The inference-time intervention introduces minimal overhead and demonstrates effectiveness across multiple model architectures, showing consistent latent patterns in response to harmful inputs.
AI.conclusion: Jailbreak behavior in LLMs is rooted in identifiable internal structures, and the proposed tensor-based latent representation framework offers a scalable, architecture-agnostic method for detecting and mitigating jailbreaks at inference time without requiring model fine-tuning or auxiliary detectors.

title: Studying Quality Improvements Recommended via Manual and Automated Code Review
comment: Accepted at the 34th International Conference on Program Comprehension (ICPC 2026)
summary: Several Deep Learning (DL)-based techniques have been proposed to automate code review. Still, it is unclear the extent to which these approaches can recommend quality improvements as a human reviewer. We study the similarities and differences between code reviews performed by humans and those automatically generated by DL models, using ChatGPT-4 as representative of the latter. In particular, we run a mining-based study in which we collect and manually inspect 739 comments posted by human reviewers to suggest code changes in 240 PRs. The manual inspection aims at classifying the type of quality improvement recommended by human reviewers (e.g., rename variable/constant). Then, we ask ChatGPT to perform a code review on the same PRs and we compare the quality improvements it recommends against those suggested by the human reviewers. We show that while, on average, ChatGPT tends to recommend a higher number of code changes as compared to human reviewers (~2.4x more), it can only spot 10% of the quality issues reported by humans. However, ~40% of the additional comments generated by the LLM point to meaningful quality issues. In short, our findings show the complementarity of manual and AI-based code review. This finding suggests that, in its current state, DL-based code review can be used as a further quality check on top of the one performed by humans, but should not be considered as a valid alternative to them nor as a mean to save code review time, since human reviewers would still need to perform their manual inspection while also validating the quality issues reported by the DL-based technique.

AI.tldr: ChatGPT-4 outperforms human reviewers in quantity of feedback but misses 90% of human-identified issues; however, many of its extra suggestions are valid, showing AI can complement but not replace human code review.
AI.motivation: There is a growing use of deep learning models for automated code review, but limited understanding of how well these systems can match human reviewers in identifying meaningful quality improvements. This study aims to assess the effectiveness and alignment of DL-based reviewers (using ChatGPT-4) with human review practices.
AI.method: A mining-based study was conducted on 240 PRs, collecting 739 human-generated review comments. These were manually classified by type of quality improvement. ChatGPT-4 was then used to generate code reviews on the same PRs, and its recommendations were compared to human comments in terms of coverage and type of issues identified.
AI.result: ChatGPT-4 suggests ~2.4x more code changes than humans but only identifies 10% of the issues flagged by humans. However, ~40% of its additional comments point to valid, previously unmentioned quality issues, demonstrating potential complementary value.
AI.conclusion: DL-based code review tools like ChatGPT-4 are not yet a substitute for human reviewers but can serve as a complementary quality check. Human reviewers still need to validate both their own and the model's suggestions, and the technology does not currently reduce review effort.

title: Differentially Private and Communication Efficient Large Language Model Split Inference via Stochastic Quantization and Soft Prompt
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance and received significant research interest. The enormous computational demands, however, hinder the local deployment on devices with limited resources. The current prevalent LLM inference paradigms require users to send queries to the service providers for processing, which raises critical privacy concerns. Existing approaches propose to allow the users to obfuscate the token embeddings before transmission and utilize local models for denoising. Nonetheless, transmitting the token embeddings and deploying local models may result in excessive communication and computation overhead, preventing practical implementation. In this work, we propose \textbf{DEL}, a framework for \textbf{D}ifferentially private and communication \textbf{E}fficient \textbf{L}LM split inference. More specifically, an embedding projection module and a differentially private stochastic quantization mechanism are proposed to reduce the communication overhead in a privacy-preserving manner. To eliminate the need for local models, we adapt soft prompt at the server side to compensate for the utility degradation caused by privacy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that utilizes soft prompt to improve the trade-off between privacy and utility in LLM inference, and extensive experiments on text generation and natural language understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: DEL enables private and efficient LLM split inference by projecting and quantizing embeddings with differential privacy, and uses server-side soft prompts—instead of local models—to maintain performance.
AI.motivation: To address privacy concerns and high communication/computation costs in current LLM inference paradigms while avoiding reliance on local models.
AI.method: DEL employs an embedding projection module and differentially private stochastic quantization to reduce communication and enhance privacy; it uses server-side soft prompts to maintain utility without requiring local models.
AI.result: DEL significantly reduces communication overhead and preserves privacy via differential privacy, with soft prompts compensating for utility loss; it shows strong performance on text generation and NLU benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: DEL is the first framework to use soft prompts for improving the privacy-utility trade-off in LLM split inference, enabling differentially private, communication-efficient, and model-free client participation.

title: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
summary:
A widespread practice in software development is to tailor coding agents to repositories using context files, such as AGENTS.md, by either manually or automatically generating them. Although this practice is strongly encouraged by agent developers, there is currently no rigorous investigation into whether such context files are actually effective for real-world tasks. In this work, we study this question and evaluate coding agents' task completion performance in two complementary settings: established SWE-bench tasks from popular repositories, with LLM-generated context files following agent-developer recommendations, and a novel collection of issues from repositories containing developer-committed context files.
  Across multiple coding agents and LLMs, we find that context files tend to reduce task success rates compared to providing no repository context, while also increasing inference cost by over 20%. Behaviorally, both LLM-generated and developer-provided context files encourage broader exploration (e.g., more thorough testing and file traversal), and coding agents tend to respect their instructions. Ultimately, we conclude that unnecessary requirements from context files make tasks harder, and human-written context files should describe only minimal requirements.

AI.tldr: Contrary to common practice, context files like AGENTS.md reduce coding agent performance and increase costs; minimal, essential instructions are recommended.
AI.motivation: Despite the common practice of using context files (e.g., AGENTS.md) to tailor coding agents to repositories, there has been no rigorous evaluation of their effectiveness. This work aims to investigate whether these context files actually improve agent performance on real-world tasks or inadvertently hinder it.
AI.method: The study evaluates coding agent performance on two settings: (1) SWE-bench tasks from popular repositories using LLM-generated context files following agent-developer guidelines, and (2) real-world issues from repositories with developer-committed context files. Multiple coding agents and LLMs are tested to assess the impact of context files on task completion, behavior, and cost.
AI.result: Context files consistently reduced task success rates compared to having no context, while increasing inference costs by over 20%. Both LLM-generated and developer-provided context files led to broader exploration behavior (e.g., more file traversal and testing), and agents generally followed the instructions. However, extraneous requirements in context files made tasks harder.
AI.conclusion: Context files, whether generated by LLMs or written by developers, tend to reduce task success rates for coding agents and increase inference costs. The study concludes that unnecessary instructions in context files make tasks harder, and recommends that human-written context files should include only minimal, essential requirements.

title: Stop Tracking Me! Proactive Defense Against Attribute Inference Attack in LLMs
summary: Recent studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can infer private user attributes (e.g., age, location, gender) from user-generated text shared online, enabling rapid and large-scale privacy breaches. Existing anonymization-based defenses are coarse-grained, lacking word-level precision in anonymizing privacy-leaking elements. Moreover, they are inherently limited as altering user text to hide sensitive cues still allows attribute inference to occur through models' reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose a unified defense framework that combines fine-grained anonymization (TRACE) with inference-preventing optimization (RPS). TRACE leverages attention mechanisms and inference chain generation to identify and anonymize privacy-leaking textual elements, while RPS employs a lightweight two-stage optimization strategy to induce model rejection behaviors, thereby preventing attribute inference. Evaluations across diverse LLMs show that TRACE-RPS reduces attribute inference accuracy from around 50\% to below 5\% on open-source models. In addition, our approach offers strong cross-model generalization, prompt-variation robustness, and utility-privacy tradeoffs. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jasper-Yan/TRACE-RPS.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TRACE-RPS, a unified defense that combines fine-grained text anonymization (TRACE) and inference-preventing optimization (RPS) to protect user privacy in LLMs, significantly reducing attribute inference accuracy while maintaining usability.
AI.motivation: Existing anonymization methods for protecting user privacy in LLMs are coarse-grained and fail to prevent inference based on textual reasoning, necessitating a more precise and effective defense mechanism against attribute leakage from user-generated text.
AI.method: TRACE uses attention mechanisms and inference chain generation to identify and anonymize privacy-leaking text elements at the word level; RPS applies a lightweight two-stage optimization to induce model rejection of attribute inference queries. The two components are integrated into a unified defense framework.
AI.result: TRACE-RPS reduces attribute inference accuracy from ~50% to below 5% on open-source LLMs, demonstrates strong generalization across models, robustness to prompt variations, and favorable utility-privacy tradeoffs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TRACE-RPS framework effectively defends against private attribute inference in LLMs by combining fine-grained anonymization and inference-preventing optimization, achieving strong privacy protection without significant utility loss.

title: An Empirical Study of the Imbalance Issue in Software Vulnerability Detection
comment: This paper was accepted by the 28th European Symposium on Research in Computer Security (ESORICS), 2023
summary: Vulnerability detection is crucial to protect software security. Nowadays, deep learning (DL) is the most promising technique to automate this detection task, leveraging its superior ability to extract patterns and representations within extensive code volumes. Despite its promise, DL-based vulnerability detection remains in its early stages, with model performance exhibiting variability across datasets. Drawing insights from other well-explored application areas like computer vision, we conjecture that the imbalance issue (the number of vulnerable code is extremely small) is at the core of the phenomenon. To validate this, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study involving nine open-source datasets and two state-of-the-art DL models. The results confirm our conjecture. We also obtain insightful findings on how existing imbalance solutions perform in vulnerability detection. It turns out that these solutions perform differently as well across datasets and evaluation metrics. Specifically: 1) Focal loss is more suitable to improve the precision, 2) mean false error and class-balanced loss encourages the recall, and 3) random over-sampling facilitates the F1-measure. However, none of them excels across all metrics. To delve deeper, we explore external influences on these solutions and offer insights for developing new solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how class imbalance impacts deep learning-based vulnerability detection through an empirical study on nine datasets and two models, showing that existing imbalance mitigation methods have metric-specific effectiveness and none dominates overall.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the observed variability in deep learning model performance across datasets in vulnerability detection, which the authors hypothesize is primarily due to class imbalance, similar to issues seen in other domains like computer vision.
AI.method: A comprehensive empirical study was conducted using nine open-source datasets and two state-of-the-art deep learning models to analyze the impact of data imbalance and evaluate the effectiveness of various imbalance mitigation techniques, including focal loss, mean false error, class-balanced loss, and random over-sampling.
AI.result: The study confirms that data imbalance is a key factor affecting model performance. Different imbalance solutions have distinct effects: focal loss improves precision, mean false error and class-balanced loss enhance recall, and random over-sampling boosts F1-measure, but no single method excels across all metrics.
AI.conclusion: The imbalance issue in vulnerability detection datasets significantly affects the performance of deep learning models, and existing imbalance solutions do not universally improve all evaluation metrics, indicating the need for more tailored and robust approaches.

title: QDBFT: A Dynamic Consensus Algorithm for Quantum-Secured Blockchain
summary:
The security foundation of blockchain system relies primarily on classical cryptographic methods and consensus algorithms. However, the advent of quantum computing poses a significant threat to conventional public-key cryptosystems based on computational hardness assumptions. In particular, Shor's algorithm can efficiently solve discrete logarithm and integer factorization problems in polynomial time, thereby undermining the immutability and security guarantees of existing systems. Moreover, current Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) protocols, widely adopted in consortium blockchains, suffer from high communication overhead and limited efficiency when coping with dynamic node reconfigurations, while offering no intrinsic protection against quantum adversaries.
  To address these challenges, we propose QDBFT, a quantum-secured dynamic consensus algorithm, with two main contributions: first,we design a primary node automatic rotation mechanism based on a consistent hash ring to enable consensus under dynamic membership changes, ensuring equitable authority distribution; second, we integrate Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks to provide message authentication for inter-node communication, thereby achieving information-theoretic security in the consensus process. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that QDBFT achieves performance comparable to traditional PBFT while delivering strong resilience against quantum attacks, making it a promising solution for future quantum-secure decentralized infrastructures.

AI.tldr: QDBFT is a quantum-secured dynamic consensus algorithm that combines a consistent hash ring for primary node rotation and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) for information-theoretically secure message authentication, offering resilience against quantum attacks while maintaining performance on par with traditional PBFT.
AI.motivation: Classical blockchain security is threatened by quantum computing, particularly through Shor's algorithm breaking public-key cryptography, and existing PBFT protocols lack efficiency in dynamic settings and quantum resistance.
AI.method: The authors design an automatic primary node rotation mechanism using a consistent hash ring for dynamic membership and integrate QKD networks to secure inter-node communication with information-theoretic security.
AI.result: Experiments show QDBFT achieves comparable performance to traditional PBFT in terms of efficiency while providing strong security against quantum adversaries.
AI.conclusion: QDBFT is a viable and secure consensus solution for future blockchain systems, effectively addressing quantum threats and dynamic node reconfiguration challenges in consortium blockchains.

title: ModelWisdom: An Integrated Toolkit for TLA+ Model Visualization, Digest and Repair
summary: Model checking in TLA+ provides strong correctness guarantees, yet practitioners continue to face significant challenges in interpreting counterexamples, understanding large state-transition graphs, and repairing faulty models. These difficulties stem from the limited explainability of raw model-checker output and the substantial manual effort required to trace violations back to source specifications. Although the TLA+ Toolbox includes a state diagram viewer, it offers only a static, fully expanded graph without folding, color highlighting, or semantic explanations, which limits its scalability and interpretability. We present ModelWisdom, an interactive environment that uses visualization and large language models to make TLA+ model checking more interpretable and actionable. ModelWisdom offers: (i) Model Visualization, with colorized violation highlighting, click-through links from transitions to TLA+ code, and mapping between violating states and broken properties; (ii) Graph Optimization, including tree-based structuring and node/edge folding to manage large models; (iii) Model Digest, which summarizes and explains subgraphs via large language models (LLMs) and performs preprocessing and partial explanations; and (iv) Model Repair, which extracts error information and supports iterative debugging. Together, these capabilities turn raw model-checker output into an interactive, explainable workflow, improving understanding and reducing debugging effort for nontrivial TLA+ specifications. The website to ModelWisdom is available: https://model-wisdom.pages.dev. A demonstrative video can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=plyZo30VShA.

AI.tldr: ModelWisdom enhances TLA+ model checking with interactive visualizations and LLM-powered explanations to make counterexamples more interpretable and debugging more efficient.
AI.motivation: Model checking in TLA+ lacks explainability and scalability in practice due to hard-to-interpret counterexamples, unwieldy state-transition graphs, and high manual effort in tracing and repairing errors, which discourages broader adoption and effective use.
AI.method: The authors introduce ModelWisdom, an interactive environment that combines enhanced visualization techniques (color highlighting, click-through links, folding) with LLM-based summarization and explanation (Model Digest) and support for iterative model repair, to address the limitations of current TLA+ debugging tools.
AI.result: ModelWisdom enables users to efficiently navigate, understand, and repair TLA+ models through structured visualizations, semantic explanations via LLMs, and integrated debugging support, reducing cognitive load and debugging time.
AI.conclusion: ModelWisdom significantly improves the interpretability and usability of TLA+ model checking by integrating interactive visualizations and large language models, enabling more effective debugging and understanding of complex specifications.

title: DMind-3: A Sovereign Edge--Local--Cloud AI System with Controlled Deliberation and Correction-Based Tuning for Safe, Low-Latency Transaction Execution
summary: This paper introduces DMind-3, a sovereign Edge-Local-Cloud intelligence stack designed to secure irreversible financial execution in Web3 environments against adversarial risks and strict latency constraints. While existing cloud-centric assistants compromise privacy and fail under network congestion, and purely local solutions lack global ecosystem context, DMind-3 resolves these tensions by decomposing capability into three cooperating layers: a deterministic signing-time intent firewall at the edge, a private high-fidelity reasoning engine on user hardware, and a policy-governed global context synthesizer in the cloud. We propose policy-driven selective offloading to route computation based on privacy sensitivity and uncertainty, supported by two novel training objectives: Hierarchical Predictive Synthesis (HPS) for fusing time-varying macro signals, and Contrastive Chain-of-Correction Supervised Fine-Tuning (C$^3$-SFT) to enhance local verification reliability. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that DMind-3 achieves a 93.7% multi-turn success rate in protocol-constrained tasks and superior domain reasoning compared to general-purpose baselines, providing a scalable framework where safety is bound to the edge execution primitive while maintaining sovereignty over sensitive user intent.

AI.tldr: DMind-3 is a sovereign Edge-Local-Cloud intelligence stack for Web3 that ensures secure, private, and low-latency financial execution by combining an edge intent firewall, local reasoning, and policy-governed cloud context with novel training methods HPS and C$^3$-SFT.
AI.motivation: Existing Web3 assistant architectures face a trade-off between privacy-preserving local execution and access to global context; cloud-only solutions are vulnerable to network issues and privacy leaks, while fully local systems lack situational awareness. DMind-3 aims to overcome this by enabling secure, low-latency, and context-aware intent processing.
AI.method: DMind-3 decomposes intelligence into three layers: an edge-based intent firewall, a local reasoning engine, and a cloud-based context synthesizer. It employs policy-driven selective offloading and introduces two novel training methods: Hierarchical Predictive Synthesis (HPS) and Contrastive Chain-of-Correction Supervised Fine-Tuning (C$^3$-SFT).
AI.result: DMind-3 achieves a 93.7% multi-turn success rate in protocol-constrained tasks and outperforms general-purpose models in domain-specific reasoning, demonstrating superior verification reliability and effective synthesis of macro-level financial signals.
AI.conclusion: DMind-3 provides a scalable, sovereign intelligence framework for Web3 by securely binding safety to edge execution while enabling global contextual awareness through policy-governed cloud coordination, thus ensuring privacy, reliability, and low-latency decision-making.

title: Performance Antipatterns: Angel or Devil for Power Consumption?
summary: Performance antipatterns are known to degrade the responsiveness of microservice-based systems, but their impact on energy consumption remains largely unexplored. This paper empirically investigates whether widely studied performance antipatterns defined by Smith and Williams also negatively influence power usage. We implement ten antipatterns as isolated microservices and evaluate them under controlled load conditions, collecting synchronized measurements of performance, CPU and DRAM power consumption, and resource utilization across 30 repeated runs per antipattern. The results show that while all antipatterns degrade performance as expected, only a subset exhibit a statistically significant relationship between response time and increased power consumption. Specifically, several antipatterns reach CPU saturation, capping power draw regardless of rising response time, whereas others (\eg Unnecessary Processing, The Ramp) demonstrate energy-performance coupling indicative of inefficiency. Our results show that, while all injected performance antipatterns increase response time as expected, only a subset also behaves as clear energy antipatterns, with several cases reaching a nearly constant CPU power level where additional slowdowns mainly translate into longer execution time rather than higher instantaneous power consumption. The study provides a systematic foundation for identifying performance antipatterns that also behave as energy antipatterns and offers actionable insights for designing more energy-efficient microservices architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the impact of performance antipatterns on energy consumption in microservice-based systems, finding that while all antipatterns degrade performance, only a subset significantly increase power consumption, with implications for energy-efficient system design.
AI.motivation: To determine whether known performance antipatterns in microservices also negatively affect energy consumption, which has not been thoroughly studied.
AI.method: Ten performance antipatterns were implemented as isolated microservices and evaluated under controlled load; synchronized metrics of performance, CPU/DRAM power, and resource utilization were collected across 30 runs per antipattern.
AI.result: All antipatterns degraded performance, but only some showed a significant link between increased response time and higher power consumption; several reached CPU saturation (capping power), while others like Unnecessary Processing and The Ramp showed clear energy-performance inefficiency.
AI.conclusion: Not all performance antipatterns are energy antipatterns; the study identifies which ones are and provides insights for building more energy-efficient microservice architectures.

title: LoRA-based Parameter-Efficient LLMs for Continuous Learning in Edge-based Malware Detection
summary: The proliferation of edge devices has created an urgent need for security solutions capable of detecting malware in real time while operating under strict computational and memory constraints. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in recognizing complex patterns, yet their deployment on edge devices remains impractical due to their resource demands. However, in edge malware detection, static or centrally retrained models degrade under evolving threats and heterogeneous traffic; locally trained models become siloed and fail to transfer across domains. To overcome these limitations, in this paper, we present a continuous learning architecture for edge-based malware detection that combines local adaptation on each device with global knowledge sharing through parameter-efficient LoRA adapters. Lightweight transformer models (DistilBERT, DistilGPT-2, TinyT5) run on edge nodes and are incrementally fine-tuned on device-specific traffic; only the resulting LoRA modules are aggregated by a lightweight coordinator and redistributed, enabling cross-device generalization without exchanging raw data. We evaluate on two public IoT security datasets, Edge-IIoTset and TON-IoT, under multi-round learning to simulate evolving threats. Compared to isolated fine-tuning, the LoRA-based exchange yields up to 20-25% accuracy gains when models encounter previously unseen attacks from another domain, while maintaining stable loss and F1 across rounds. LoRA adds less than 1% to model size (~0.6-1.8 MB), making updates practical for constrained edge hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a parameter-efficient, continuous learning framework for edge-based malware detection using LoRA adapters, enabling lightweight transformers to adapt locally and share knowledge globally without exchanging raw data, achieving significant accuracy gains under low resource overhead.
AI.motivation: Edge devices require real-time, adaptive malware detection under stringent resource constraints. Conventional centralized or static models fail to adapt to evolving threats and domain shifts, while full model retraining and data sharing are impractical due to privacy, bandwidth, and computational limitations.
AI.method: A decentralized continuous learning framework is introduced, where lightweight transformer models (DistilBERT, DistilGPT-2, TinyT5) are locally fine-tuned on edge devices using LoRA adapters. Only LoRA parameters are transmitted to a coordinator for aggregation and redistribution, enabling global knowledge sharing while preserving privacy and reducing communication costs.
AI.result: The approach achieves up to 20–25% higher accuracy in detecting unseen cross-domain attacks compared to isolated fine-tuning, maintains stable loss and F1 scores over multiple learning rounds, and adds less than 1% overhead in model size (0.6–1.8 MB) due to LoRA's parameter efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed continuous learning architecture using LoRA adapters enables effective and efficient edge-based malware detection with strong cross-device generalization, minimal memory overhead, and no raw data exchange, making it well-suited for resource-constrained and evolving IoT environments.

title: PPTAM$η$: Energy Aware CI/CD Pipeline for Container Based Applications
summary: Modern container-based microservices evolve through rapid deployment cycles, but CI/CD pipelines still rarely measure energy consumption, even though prior work shows that design patterns, code smells and refactorings affect energy efficiency. We present PPTAM$η$, an automated pipeline that integrates power and energy measurement into GitLab CI for containerised API systems, coordinating load generation, container monitoring and hardware power probes to collect comparable metrics at each commit. The pipeline makes energy visible to developers, supports version comparison for test engineers and enables trend analysis for researchers. We evaluate PPTAM$η$ on a JWT-authenticated API across four commits, collecting performance and energy metrics and summarising the architecture, measurement methodology and validation.

AI.tldr: PPTAM$\eta$ is an automated GitLab CI pipeline that integrates power and energy measurement for containerized API systems, enabling energy-aware development through commit-level monitoring, version comparison, and trend analysis.
AI.motivation: Energy efficiency in container-based microservices is often overlooked in CI/CD pipelines despite the known impact of code changes on energy consumption. There is a need to make energy usage visible during development to support sustainable software engineering.
AI.method: The authors designed PPTAM$\eta$, a pipeline that integrates hardware power probes, container monitoring, and load generation into GitLab CI. It automatically collects and correlates performance and energy metrics at each commit for containerized JWT-authenticated API services.
AI.result: PPTAM$\eta$ was evaluated across four commits of a JWT-authenticated API, demonstrating consistent collection of comparable energy and performance metrics. The system successfully enables per-commit energy measurement, version-to-version comparison, and architectural validation.
AI.conclusion: Integrating energy measurement into CI/CD pipelines is feasible and valuable. PPTAM$\eta$ provides a practical framework for developers, testers, and researchers to monitor and improve the energy efficiency of containerized microservices.

title: Reliable and Private Anonymous Routing for Satellite Constellations
summary: Shared, dynamic network infrastructures, such as dual-use LEO satellite constellations, pose critical threats to metadata privacy, particularly for state actors operating in mixed-trust environments. This work proposes an enhanced anonymity architecture, evolving the Loopix mix-network, to provide robust security and reliability in these volatile topologies. We introduce three primary contributions: (1) A multi-path transport protocol utilizing $(n, k)$ erasure codes, which is demonstrated to counteract the high link volatility and intermittent connectivity that renders standard mix-networks unreliable. (2) The integration of a computationally efficient Private Information Retrieval (PIR) protocol during route discovery. (3) The introduction of adaptive, centrality-based delay strategies that efficiently mitigate the inherent topological bias of LEO networks, providing a superior anonymity-to-latency trade-off. This mechanism provably prevents metadata leakage at the user-provider directory, mitigating profiling and correlation attacks. We validate this architecture via high-fidelity, packet-level simulations of a LEO constellation. Empirical results show our multi-path transport achieves near-zero message loss, establishing a quantifiable trade-off between reliability and bandwidth overhead. Furthermore, microbenchmarks of the PIR protocol quantify its computational and latency overheads, confirming its feasibility for practical deployment. This work provides a validated blueprint for deployable high-anonymity communication systems, demonstrating the viability of securely multiplexing sensitive operations within large-scale commercial network infrastructures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an enhanced anonymity architecture for LEO satellite networks by extending Loopix with erasure-coded multi-path transport, efficient PIR for route discovery, and adaptive delay strategies, achieving robust metadata privacy and reliability in high-volatility environments.
AI.motivation: Dual-use LEO satellite constellations and similar shared, dynamic network infrastructures introduce critical metadata privacy risks, especially for state actors in mixed-trust environments. Standard mix-networks fail in such volatile topologies due to high link instability and topological biases, necessitating a robust, reliable, and anonymous communication architecture.
AI.method: The authors propose an enhanced anonymity architecture based on the Loopix mix-network, incorporating (1) a multi-path transport protocol using $(n, k)$ erasure codes for resilience to link volatility, (2) integration of a computationally efficient Private Information Retrieval (PIR) protocol during route discovery to protect metadata, and (3) adaptive, centrality-based delay strategies to counter topological bias and improve the anonymity-to-latency trade-off. The system is evaluated through high-fidelity, packet-level simulations of a LEO satellite constellation.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves near-zero message loss under high link volatility due to the multi-path erasure-coded transport. The PIR protocol is shown to be feasible for practical deployment with quantifiable computational and latency overheads. The adaptive delay mechanisms effectively mitigate topological bias, improving anonymity while maintaining acceptable latency. Packet-level simulations confirm the system's reliability, security, and effectiveness in preventing metadata leakage and correlation attacks.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a validated blueprint for deployable high-anonymity communication systems, demonstrating the viability of securely multiplexing sensitive operations within large-scale commercial network infrastructures, particularly in dual-use LEO satellite constellations.

title: On the Adoption of AI Coding Agents in Open-source Android and iOS Development
comment: Accepted at MSR 2026 Mining Challenge track
summary: AI coding agents are increasingly contributing to software development, yet their impact on mobile development has received little empirical attention. In this paper, we present the first category-level empirical study of agent-generated code in open-source mobile app projects. We analyzed PR acceptance behaviors across mobile platforms, agents, and task categories using 2,901 AI-authored pull requests (PRs) in 193 verified Android and iOS open-source GitHub repositories in the AIDev dataset. We find that Android projects have received 2x more AI-authored PRs and have achieved higher PR acceptance rate (71%) than iOS (63%), with significant agent-level variation on Android. Across task categories, PRs with routine tasks (feature, fix, and ui) achieve the highest acceptance, while structural changes like refactor and build achieve lower success and longer resolution times. Furthermore, our evolution analysis shows improvement in PR resolution time on Android through mid-2025 before it declined again. Our findings offer the first evidence-based characterization of AI agents effects on OSS mobile projects and establish empirical baselines for evaluating agent-generated contributions to design platform aware agentic systems.

AI.tldr: First empirical study on AI coding agents in mobile OSS shows Android favors AI contributions more than iOS, with higher acceptance for routine tasks and evolving temporal patterns in PR resolution.
AI.motivation: Despite growing use of AI coding agents in software development, their impact on mobile app development—particularly across platforms and task types—lacks empirical investigation. This study aims to fill that gap by providing the first large-scale, category-level empirical analysis of AI-generated code integration in open-source mobile projects.
AI.method: The study conducts a category-level empirical analysis of 2,901 AI-authored pull requests (PRs) from 193 verified open-source Android and iOS GitHub repositories in the AIDev dataset. It examines PR acceptance rates, resolution times, and variations across platforms (Android vs. iOS), AI agents, and task categories (e.g., feature, fix, ui, refactor, build), including temporal evolution analysis up to mid-2025.
AI.result: Android projects received twice as many AI-authored PRs as iOS and showed a higher PR acceptance rate (71% vs. 63%) with notable variation among agents. Routine task PRs (feature, fix, ui) had the highest acceptance and faster resolution, while refactor and build tasks had lower success and longer resolution times. PR resolution time on Android improved until mid-2025 before declining, indicating fluctuating developer responsiveness or agent performance.
AI.conclusion: This paper concludes that AI coding agents have a more significant presence and higher acceptance rate in Android open-source projects compared to iOS, with routine tasks being more readily accepted than structural changes. The study establishes empirical baselines for understanding how AI-generated code is integrated into mobile development and highlights the need for platform-aware agentic systems.

title: More Haste, Less Speed: Weaker Single-Layer Watermark Improves Distortion-Free Watermark Ensembles
summary: Watermarking has emerged as a crucial technique for detecting and attributing content generated by large language models. While recent advancements have utilized watermark ensembles to enhance robustness, prevailing methods typically prioritize maximizing the strength of the watermark at every individual layer. In this work, we identify a critical limitation in this "stronger-is-better" approach: strong watermarks significantly reduce the entropy of the token distribution, which paradoxically weakens the effectiveness of watermarking in subsequent layers. We theoretically and empirically show that detectability is bounded by entropy and that watermark ensembles induce a monotonic decrease in both entropy and the expected green-list ratio across layers. To address this inherent trade-off, we propose a general framework that utilizes weaker single-layer watermarks to preserve the entropy required for effective multi-layer ensembling. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this counter-intuitive strategy mitigates signal decay and consistently outperforms strong baselines in both detectability and robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the 'stronger-is-better' paradigm in LLM watermarking, showing that strong watermarks reduce token entropy and degrade multi-layer performance; it proposes a framework using weaker watermarks to preserve entropy and improve detectability and robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing watermark ensembles in LLMs focus on maximizing per-layer watermark strength, but this can reduce token distribution entropy, undermining detectability in deeper layers. The authors aim to understand and resolve this trade-off between watermark strength and entropy preservation.
AI.method: The authors analyze the relationship between watermark strength, entropy, and green-list token ratios across layers. They propose a new framework that applies weaker watermarks at individual layers to maintain higher entropy, enabling more effective multi-layer ensembling and avoiding signal decay.
AI.result: Theoretical and empirical results show that strong watermarks monotonically reduce entropy and green-list ratios across layers. The proposed weaker-watermark framework mitigates entropy loss, reduces signal decay, and outperforms strong watermark baselines in detectability and robustness under various attacks.
AI.conclusion: Preserving entropy via weaker single-layer watermarks enables more effective multi-layer ensembling. This counter-intuitive approach achieves superior performance, challenging the conventional emphasis on maximizing per-layer watermark strength.

title: Automated Test Suite Enhancement Using Large Language Models with Few-shot Prompting
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, accepted to ICPC 2026 (34th International Conference on Program Comprehension)
summary: Unit testing is essential for verifying the functional correctness of code modules (e.g., classes, methods), but manually writing unit tests is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. Unit tests generated by tools that employ traditional approaches, such as search-based software testing (SBST), lack readability, naturalness, and practical usability. LLMs have recently provided promising results and become integral to developers' daily practices. Consequently, software repositories now include a mix of human-written tests, LLM-generated tests, and those from tools employing traditional approaches such as SBST. While LLMs' zero-shot capabilities have been widely studied, their few-shot learning potential for unit test generation remains underexplored. Few-shot prompting enables LLMs to learn from examples in the prompt, and automatically retrieving such examples could enhance test suites. This paper empirically investigates how few-shot prompting with different test artifact sources, comprising human, SBST, or LLM, affects the quality of LLM-generated unit tests as program comprehension artifacts and their contribution to improving existing test suites by evaluating not only correctness and coverage but also readability, cognitive complexity, and maintainability in hybrid human-AI codebases. We conducted experiments on HumanEval and ClassEval datasets using GPT-4o, which is integrated into GitHub Copilot and widely used among developers. We also assessed retrieval-based methods for selecting relevant examples. Our results show that LLMs can generate high-quality tests via few-shot prompting, with human-written examples producing the best coverage and correctness. Additionally, selecting examples based on the combined similarity of problem description and code consistently yields the most effective few-shot prompts.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates few-shot LLM-based unit test generation using human, SBST, and LLM-generated examples, showing that human-written examples and combined similarity-based retrieval yield the highest test quality in hybrid development environments.
AI.motivation: To explore the underexplored few-shot learning capability of LLMs in unit test generation and improve the quality of generated tests in hybrid human-AI codebases by leveraging diverse test artifact sources.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of few-shot prompting using GPT-4o on HumanEval and ClassEval datasets, comparing test generation performance with examples from human, SBST, and LLM sources; assessment of retrieval-based methods based on code and problem description similarity.
AI.result: LLM-generated unit tests using few-shot prompting achieve high quality, with human-written examples yielding superior correctness and coverage; retrieval based on combined problem description and code similarity produces the most effective prompts.
AI.conclusion: Few-shot prompting of LLMs, especially with human-written test examples, significantly enhances the quality of generated unit tests in terms of correctness, coverage, readability, and maintainability; combining problem description and code similarity improves example retrieval effectiveness.

title: Solving the Post-Quantum Control Plane Bottleneck: Energy-Aware Cryptographic Scheduling in Open RAN
summary: The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) offers flexibility and innovation but introduces unique security vulnerabilities, particularly from cryptographically relevant quantum computers. While Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is the primary scalable defence, its computationally intensive handshakes create a significant bottleneck for the RAN control plane, posing sustainability challenges. This paper proposes an energy-aware framework to solve this PQC bottleneck, ensuring quantum resilience without sacrificing operational energy efficiency. The system employs an O-RAN aligned split: a Crypto Policy rApp residing in the Non-Real-Time (Non-RT) RIC defines the strategic security envelope (including PQC suites), while a Security Operations Scheduling (SOS) xApp in the Near-RT RIC converts these into tactical timing and placement intents. Cryptographic enforcement remains at standards-compliant endpoints: the Open Fronthaul utilizes Media Access Control Security (MACsec) at the O-DU/O-RU, while the xhaul (midhaul and backhaul) utilizes IP Security (IPsec) at tunnel terminators. The SOS xApp reduces PQC overhead by batching non-urgent handshakes, prioritizing session resumption, and selecting parameters that meet slice SLAs while minimizing joules per secure connection. We evaluate the architecture via a Discrete-Event Simulation (DES) using 3GPP-aligned traffic profiles and verified hardware benchmarks from literature. Results show that intelligent scheduling can reduce per-handshake energy by approximately 60 percent without violating slice latency targets.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an energy-aware, O-RAN-integrated security framework that alleviates the computational burden of post-quantum cryptography in mobile networks by intelligently scheduling cryptographic handshakes across the Non-RT and Near-RT RICs, achieving up to 60% reduction in energy per handshake while preserving quantum resilience and slice-specific latency requirements.
AI.motivation: The integration of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RAN) is critical for future-proofing against quantum threats, but the high computational cost of PQC handshakes introduces significant energy inefficiency and control plane bottlenecks, threatening operational sustainability. Existing approaches fail to balance security and energy efficiency in dynamic, slice-aware RAN environments.
AI.method: An O-RAN-compliant split architecture is designed, where a Crypto Policy rApp in the Non-RT RIC sets high-level security policies including PQC suite selection, and a Security Operations Scheduling (SOS) xApp in the Near-RT RIC translates these into operational scheduling decisions. PQC overhead is reduced via handshake batching, session resumption prioritization, and energy-optimal parameter selection. Cryptographic enforcement is maintained at standard endpoints using MACsec for open fronthaul and IPsec for xhaul links. The system is evaluated using a Discrete-Event Simulation (DES) with 3GPP-aligned traffic models and real hardware performance benchmarks.
AI.result: The evaluation shows that the proposed SOS xApp reduces per-handshake energy consumption by approximately 60% compared to baseline PQC deployment, while maintaining compliance with latency requirements across network slices. The framework demonstrates scalability and energy efficiency without degrading security or violating SLAs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed energy-aware O-RAN security framework effectively mitigates the computational and energy overhead of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) in RAN control planes by leveraging intelligent, split-architecture scheduling, thus achieving quantum resilience without compromising energy efficiency or violating service-level agreements.

title: Resource-Aware Deployment Optimization for Collaborative Intrusion Detection in Layered Networks
summary: Collaborative Intrusion Detection Systems (CIDS) are increasingly adopted to counter cyberattacks, as their collaborative nature enables them to adapt to diverse scenarios across heterogeneous environments. As distributed critical infrastructure operates in rapidly evolving environments, such as drones in both civil and military domains, there is a growing need for CIDS architectures that can flexibly accommodate these dynamic changes. In this study, we propose a novel CIDS framework designed for easy deployment across diverse distributed environments. The framework dynamically optimizes detector allocation per node based on available resources and data types, enabling rapid adaptation to new operational scenarios with minimal computational overhead. We first conducted a comprehensive literature review to identify key characteristics of existing CIDS architectures. Based on these insights and real-world use cases, we developed our CIDS framework, which we evaluated using several distributed datasets that feature different attack chains and network topologies. Notably, we introduce a public dataset based on a realistic cyberattack targeting a ground drone aimed at sabotaging critical infrastructure. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CIDS framework can achieve adaptive, efficient intrusion detection in distributed settings, automatically reconfiguring detectors to maintain an optimal configuration, without requiring heavy computation, since all experiments were conducted on edge devices.

AI.tldr: A novel Collaborative Intrusion Detection System (CIDS) framework is proposed for dynamic, resource-aware deployment in distributed environments, enabling adaptive and efficient intrusion detection with minimal overhead on edge devices.
AI.motivation: The increasing complexity and heterogeneity of distributed critical infrastructures, such as drone systems in civil and military domains, demand flexible and adaptive CIDS architectures capable of evolving alongside dynamic threat landscapes and operational conditions.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comprehensive literature review to identify limitations in existing CIDS architectures. They designed a novel CIDS framework that dynamically allocates detectors based on node resources and data types. The system was evaluated using multiple distributed datasets with varied attack chains and topologies, including a newly introduced public dataset simulating a realistic cyberattack on a ground drone targeting critical infrastructure.
AI.result: The proposed framework demonstrated adaptive and efficient intrusion detection in distributed settings, automatically reconfiguring detectors to maintain optimal performance. All experiments were successfully run on edge devices, confirming low computational overhead and practical deployability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CIDS framework enables lightweight, dynamic, and context-aware intrusion detection across heterogeneous distributed systems, making it suitable for real-time deployment in resource-constrained environments such as edge-based drone networks.

title: Agentic AI for Cybersecurity: A Meta-Cognitive Architecture for Governable Autonomy
summary: Contemporary AI-driven cybersecurity systems are predominantly architected as model-centric detection and automation pipelines optimized for task-level performance metrics such as accuracy and response latency. While effective for bounded classification tasks, these architectures struggle to support accountable decision-making under adversarial uncertainty, where actions must be justified, governed, and aligned with organizational and regulatory constraints. This paper argues that cybersecurity orchestration should be reconceptualized as an agentic, multi-agent cognitive system, rather than a linear sequence of detection and response components. We introduce a conceptual architectural framework in which heterogeneous AI agents responsible for detection, hypothesis formation, contextual interpretation, explanation, and governance are coordinated through an explicit meta-cognitive judgement function. This function governs decision readiness and dynamically calibrates system autonomy when evidence is incomplete, conflicting, or operationally risky. By synthesizing distributed cognition theory, multi-agent systems research, and responsible AI governance frameworks, we demonstrate that modern security operations already function as distributed cognitive systems, albeit without an explicit organizing principle. Our contribution is to make this cognitive structure architecturally explicit and governable by embedding meta-cognitive judgement as a first-class system function. We discuss implications for security operations centers, accountable autonomy, and the design of next-generation AI-enabled cyber defence architectures. The proposed framework shifts the focus of AI in cybersecurity from optimizing isolated predictions to governing autonomy under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a meta-cognitive, multi-agent architecture for AI-driven cybersecurity that shifts from model-centric detection to governed autonomy, enabling accountable decision-making under uncertainty through explicit cognitive coordination and judgment functions.
AI.motivation: Contemporary model-centric AI systems in cybersecurity focus on task performance but lack support for accountable, justifiable, and governed decisions under adversarial uncertainty; this gap motivates a reconceptualization of cybersecurity orchestration as an agentic, multi-agent cognitive system.
AI.method: The paper develops a conceptual architectural framework based on distributed cognition theory, multi-agent systems, and responsible AI governance, in which heterogeneous AI agents are coordinated through a meta-cognitive judgment function that evaluates decision readiness and calibrates autonomy dynamically.
AI.result: The framework formalizes security operations as an explicit distributed cognitive system, demonstrating how meta-cognitive judgement can govern AI autonomy, improve decision justification, and align actions with regulatory and organizational constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework shifts AI in cybersecurity from isolated prediction optimization to governing autonomy under uncertainty by introducing meta-cognitive judgement as a first-class architectural component, enabling accountable, interpretable, and organizationally aligned decision-making in security operations.

title: Unknown Attack Detection in IoT Networks using Large Language Models: A Robust, Data-efficient Approach
summary: The rapid evolution of cyberattacks continues to drive the emergence of unknown (zero-day) threats, posing significant challenges for network intrusion detection systems in Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Existing machine learning and deep learning approaches typically rely on large labeled datasets, payload inspection, or closed-set classification, limiting their effectiveness under data scarcity, encrypted traffic, and distribution shifts. Consequently, detecting unknown attacks in realistic IoT deployments remains difficult. To address these limitations, we propose SiamXBERT, a robust and data-efficient Siamese meta-learning framework empowered by a transformer-based language model for unknown attack detection. The proposed approach constructs a dual-modality feature representation by integrating flow-level and packet-level information, enabling richer behavioral modeling while remaining compatible with encrypted traffic. Through meta-learning, the model rapidly adapts to new attack types using only a small number of labeled samples and generalizes to previously unseen behaviors. Extensive experiments on representative IoT intrusion datasets demonstrate that SiamXBERT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under both within-dataset and cross-dataset settings while requiring significantly less training data, achieving up to \num{78.8}\% improvement in unknown F1-score. These results highlight the practicality of SiamXBERT for robust unknown attack detection in real-world IoT environments.

AI.tldr: SiamXBERT is a data-efficient, transformer-based meta-learning framework for detecting unknown attacks in IoT networks using dual-modality traffic features, showing superior performance with minimal labeled data.
AI.motivation: Existing intrusion detection systems struggle with zero-day attacks due to reliance on large labeled datasets, payload inspection, and closed-set classification, which limits their performance in real-world IoT environments with encrypted traffic and distribution shifts.
AI.method: The authors propose SiamXBERT, a Siamese meta-learning framework powered by a transformer-based language model that uses dual-modality feature representation (flow-level and packet-level) for zero-day attack detection.
AI.result: SiamXBERT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both within-dataset and cross-dataset evaluations, achieving up to 78.8% improvement in unknown F1-score with significantly less training data.
AI.conclusion: SiamXBERT is a practical and robust solution for detecting unknown cyberattacks in IoT networks, particularly under data scarcity and encrypted traffic conditions.

title: PAC to the Future: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of PAC Private Systems
summary: Privacy concerns in machine learning systems have grown significantly with the increasing reliance on sensitive user data for training large-scale models. This paper introduces a novel framework combining Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Privacy with zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to provide verifiable privacy guarantees in trustless computing environments. Our approach addresses the limitations of traditional privacy-preserving techniques by enabling users to verify both the correctness of computations and the proper application of privacy-preserving noise, particularly in cloud-based systems. We leverage non-interactive ZKP schemes to generate proofs that attest to the correct implementation of PAC privacy mechanisms while maintaining the confidentiality of proprietary systems. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of achieving verifiable PAC privacy in outsourced computation, offering a practical solution for maintaining trust in privacy-preserving machine learning and database systems while ensuring computational integrity.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a verifiable privacy framework by combining PAC Privacy with zero-knowledge proofs, enabling users to confirm correct privacy enforcement in outsourced computations without compromising data or system confidentiality.
AI.motivation: Traditional privacy-preserving methods lack verifiability in trustless environments, especially when computations are outsourced, leading to potential misuse or incorrect implementation of privacy mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel framework that integrates PAC Privacy with non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to allow verification of both computational correctness and correct application of privacy-preserving noise in cloud-based systems.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates feasibility in practice by enabling efficient verification of PAC privacy compliance without revealing sensitive or proprietary information, thereby ensuring both privacy and computational integrity.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that combining PAC Privacy with zero-knowledge proofs enables verifiable and trustworthy privacy guarantees in outsourced, trustless environments, making it a viable approach for privacy-preserving machine learning and database systems.

title: Evaluation of Security-Induced Latency on 5G RAN Interfaces and User Plane Communication
summary: 5G promises enhanced performance-not only in bandwidth and capacity, but also latency and security. Its ultra-reliable low-latency configuration targets round-trip times below 1 ms, while optional security controls extend protection across all interfaces, making 5G attractive for mission-critical applications. A key enabler of low latency is the disaggregation of network components, including the RAN, allowing user-plane functions to be deployed nearer to end users. However, this split introduces additional interfaces, whose protection increases latency overhead. In this paper, guided by discussions with a network operator and a 5G manufacturer, we evaluate the latency overhead of enabling optional 5G security controls across internal RAN interfaces and the 5G user plane. To this end, we deploy the first testbed implementing a disaggregated RAN with standardized optional security mechanisms. Our results show that disaggregated RAN deployments retain a latency advantage over monolithic designs, even with security enabled. However, achieving sub-1 ms round-trip times remains challenging, as cryptographic overhead alone can already exceed this target.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the latency impact of optional 5G security in disaggregated RANs using a real testbed; findings show that while disaggregation reduces latency, cryptographic overhead can prevent achieving sub-1 ms round-trip times.
AI.motivation: To assess the impact of optional 5G security controls on latency in disaggregated RAN architectures, which are critical for ultra-reliable low-latency communication, especially in mission-critical applications.
AI.method: The authors deployed the first testbed implementing a disaggregated RAN with standardized optional security mechanisms and evaluated the latency overhead of enabling these security controls across internal RAN interfaces and the 5G user plane, based on discussions with a network operator and a 5G manufacturer.
AI.result: The testbed results show that security-enabled disaggregated RANs still outperform monolithic designs in latency, but cryptographic processing alone can exceed the 1 ms round-trip time target, making sub-1 ms performance challenging.
AI.conclusion: Disaggregated RAN deployments maintain a latency advantage over monolithic designs even with optional 5G security mechanisms enabled, but achieving sub-1 ms round-trip times is difficult due to cryptographic overhead.

title: MedExChain: Enabling Secure and Efffcient PHR Sharing Across Heterogeneous Blockchains
summary: With the proliferation of intelligent healthcare systems, patients' Personal Health Records (PHR) generated by the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) in real-time play a vital role in disease diagnosis. The integration of emerging blockchain technologies signiffcantly enhanced the data security inside intelligent medical systems. However, data sharing across different systems based on varied blockchain architectures is still constrained by the unsolved performance and security challenges. This paper constructs a cross-chain data sharing scheme, termed MedExChain, which aims to securely share PHR across heterogeneous blockchain systems. The MedExChain scheme ensures that PHR can be shared across chains even under the performance limitations of IoMT devices. Additionally, the scheme incorporates Cryptographic Reverse Firewall (CRF) and a blockchain audit mechanism to defend against both internal and external security threats. The robustness of our scheme is validated through BAN logic, Scyther tool, Chosen Plaintext Attack (CPA) and Algorithm Substitution Attack (ASA) security analysis veriffcation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MedExChain signiffcantly minimizes computation and communication overhead, making it suitable for IoMT devices and fostering the efffcient circulation of PHR across diverse blockchain systems.

AI.tldr: MedExChain is a cross-chain scheme for secure and efficient sharing of Personal Health Records in heterogeneous blockchain-based healthcare systems, designed for IoMT constraints and enhanced with CRF and audit mechanisms for security.
AI.motivation: The increasing use of IoMT devices generates real-time Personal Health Records, and while blockchain enhances security, data sharing across different blockchain architectures remains hindered by performance and security limitations.
AI.method: The paper proposes MedExChain, a cross-chain data sharing scheme leveraging blockchain technology, Cryptographic Reverse Firewall (CRF), and a blockchain audit mechanism to ensure secure and lightweight data exchange. Formal security analyses are conducted using BAN logic, Scyther, CPA, and ASA.
AI.result: MedExChain reduces computation and communication overhead significantly, maintains security under internal and external threats, and demonstrates robustness through formal verification and extensive evaluation.
AI.conclusion: MedExChain provides a secure and efficient solution for cross-chain sharing of Personal Health Records across heterogeneous blockchain systems, particularly suitable for resource-constrained IoMT devices.

title: BlackCATT: Black-box Collusion Aware Traitor Tracing in Federated Learning
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (TIFS) for possible publication
summary: Federated Learning has been popularized in recent years for applications involving personal or sensitive data, as it allows the collaborative training of machine learning models through local updates at the data-owners' premises, which does not require the sharing of the data itself. Considering the risk of leakage or misuse by any of the data-owners, many works attempt to protect their copyright, or even trace the origin of a potential leak through unique watermarks identifying each participant's model copy. Realistic accusation scenarios impose a black-box setting, where watermarks are typically embedded as a set of sample-label pairs. The threat of collusion, however, where multiple bad actors conspire together to produce an untraceable model, has been rarely addressed, and previous works have been limited to shallow networks and near-linearly separable main tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to present a general collusion-resistant embedding method for black-box traitor tracing in Federated Learning: BlackCATT, which introduces a novel collusion-aware embedding loss term and, instead of using a fixed trigger set, iteratively optimizes the triggers to aid convergence and traitor tracing performance. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of the proposed scheme across different architectures and datasets. Furthermore, for models that would otherwise suffer from update incompatibility on the main task after learning different watermarks (e.g., architectures including batch normalization layers), our proposed BlackCATT+FR incorporates functional regularization through a set of auxiliary examples at the aggregator, promoting a shared feature space among model copies without compromising traitor tracing performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes BlackCATT, the first general framework for collusion-resistant, black-box traitor tracing in Federated Learning, using adaptive trigger optimization and a collusion-aware loss; it introduces BlackCATT+FR with functional regularization to ensure model compatibility during watermarking, demonstrating robust performance across architectures and datasets.
AI.motivation: While watermarking in Federated Learning enables traitor tracing in black-box settings, collusion among malicious participants poses a significant threat by enabling them to remove or obscure watermarks. Existing methods fail under realistic collusion scenarios and are limited to simple models and tasks, necessitating a robust, generalizable solution.
AI.method: BlackCATT introduces a novel collusion-aware embedding loss and iteratively optimizes watermark triggers instead of using fixed trigger sets to improve convergence and tracing robustness. BlackCATT+FR adds functional regularization via auxiliary examples at the aggregator to align feature spaces across clients, ensuring compatibility with difficult architectures.
AI.result: Experiments show that BlackCATT achieves strong traitor tracing performance across various architectures and datasets under collusion attacks. BlackCATT+FR successfully mitigates update incompatibility issues in models with batch normalization, preserving both main task performance and watermark detectability.
AI.conclusion: BlackCATT is the first general collusion-resistant watermarking method for black-box traitor tracing in Federated Learning, effectively identifying malicious participants even under collusion; BlackCATT+FR extends this approach by incorporating functional regularization to maintain model compatibility during watermark training, especially in architectures with batch normalization.

title: MalTool: Malicious Tool Attacks on LLM Agents
summary:
In a malicious tool attack, an attacker uploads a malicious tool to a distribution platform; once a user installs the tool and the LLM agent selects it during task execution, the tool can compromise the user's security and privacy. Prior work primarily focuses on manipulating tool names and descriptions to increase the likelihood of installation by users and selection by LLM agents. However, a successful attack also requires embedding malicious behaviors in the tool's code implementation, which remains largely unexplored.
  In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting the first systematic study of malicious tool code implementations. We first propose a taxonomy of malicious tool behaviors based on the confidentiality-integrity-availability triad, tailored to LLM-agent settings. To investigate the severity of the risks posed by attackers exploiting coding LLMs to automatically generate malicious tools, we develop MalTool, a coding-LLM-based framework that synthesizes tools exhibiting specified malicious behaviors, either as standalone tools or embedded within otherwise benign implementations. To ensure functional correctness and structural diversity, MalTool leverages an automated verifier that validates whether generated tools exhibit the intended malicious behaviors and differ sufficiently from prior instances, iteratively refining generations until success. Our evaluation demonstrates that MalTool is highly effective even when coding LLMs are safety-aligned. Using MalTool, we construct two datasets of malicious tools: 1,200 standalone malicious tools and 5,287 real-world tools with embedded malicious behaviors. We further show that existing detection methods, including commercial malware detection approaches such as VirusTotal and methods tailored to the LLM-agent setting, exhibit limited effectiveness at detecting the malicious tools, highlighting an urgent need for new defenses.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic study of malicious code in LLM agent tools, introducing a taxonomy and MalTool—a framework that uses coding LLMs to generate functionally correct and structurally diverse malicious tools—demonstrating that current detection methods are insufficient.
AI.motivation: Prior work on malicious tool attacks in LLM-agent systems focused on social engineering via tool names and descriptions, while the critical aspect of malicious code implementation remained unexplored.
AI.method: Developed MalTool, a coding-LLM-based framework that generates malicious tools with specified behaviors, using an automated verifier to ensure functional correctness, structural diversity, and iterative refinement; constructed two datasets of malicious tools for evaluation.
AI.result: MalTool successfully generates malicious code even with safety-aligned coding LLMs; produced 1,200 standalone malicious tools and 5,287 real-world tools with embedded malicious behaviors; evaluation shows existing detection methods fail to identify most of these tools.
AI.conclusion: Existing detection methods, including commercial malware detectors and LLM-agent-specific approaches, are ineffective against malicious tool code generated by coding LLMs, indicating an urgent need for improved defenses.

title: Keeping a Secret Requires a Good Memory: Space Lower-Bounds for Private Algorithms
summary:
We study the computational cost of differential privacy in terms of memory efficiency.
